newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl, Rexrodt differ on German jobless outlook.
newsitem.headline: Kohl, Rexrodt differ on German jobless outlook.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and his economics minister Guenter Rexrodt, in separate weekend interviews, gave sharply differing forecasts about prospects for cutting the country's stubbornly high jobless rate
While the Christian Democrat Chancellor was upbeat, Rexrodt, of the junior coalition partner Free Democrats, was gloomy.
Chances of a significant cut in unemployment were bleak in spite of forecasts that economic growth will pick up next year, Rexrodt told German radio.
"This year the German job market situation is still alarmingly bad and next year only a small improvement is expected," he said.
Germany's unemployment rate stands at 10.4 percent -- nearly four million people -- and is close to a post-World War Two high.
Kohl, in an interview with the Hannoversche Allgemeine Zeitung, was more optimistic, suggesting unemployment could be halved by the year 2000.
Recalling successful job creation in West Germany in the early 1980s, Kohl asked: "Why shouldn't such a thing occur again if we all roll up our sleeves?"
Both Kohl and Rexrodt predicted economic growth would pick up to about 2.5 percent in 1997. Rexrodt said he saw growth this year at above one percent, saying the economic downturn was over.
Stable prices and moderate wage agreements in the coming years will support economic growth, Rexrodt said.
Kohl acknowledged that an economic upturn was no longer enough to automatically reduce unemployment. "We have to generate a few more ideas," Kohl said.
Greater job market flexibility, including more part-time work and a greater willingess among young people to run their own firms, would be steps in the right direction, the chancellor said.
Two regional governments disagreed with Kohl, however, saying the goal was too ambitious.
The governments of Bavaria and Saxony expressed doubts that unemployment could be cut significantly in the next few years.
